archetype.name: Rebuilding (first-year coach, QB in flux)
archetype.definition: A team in Mike LaFleur's first season that has finished near the bottom in most recent years, still has no settled quarterback, and is playing out the year with a pass defense that cannot hold up.

report.headline: Since the quarterback switch, a competitive loser has become a blowout loser.
report.take:
This is the same Arizona team the last few seasons have produced, under a new coach. The 2025 club went 3-14 with a pass defense ranked 26th by EPA. The 2023 team went 4-13 with a defense ranked 31st. The 2026 version is 3-8 and has been outscored by 132 points. Its point differential implies 2.6 wins, so the record is not hiding a better team, and it is not unluckily worse than its play either. It is roughly what it has earned.

The season splits cleanly at the quarterback position. Jacoby Brissett started the first eight games, and in that stretch the offense could keep pace. It scored 30 at San Francisco, 33 at Dallas with 202 rushing yards, and won a grinder in Los Angeles. All three wins came in his starts. Then the job went to Gardner Minshew for two weeks and Josh Johnson for one, and the scoring dried up: 3 at Seattle, 6 against the Rams, 7 at Kansas City. The Rams game was the low point, at -13.5 passing EPA and 34 rushing yards. Carson Beck is now listed out with back spasms, so it is not even clear who takes the next snap.

The numbers hide some of this. The efficiency table looks like it has not caught up to the whole season: it shows a 3-6 team scoring 19.8 a game, while the game log has them at 17.4 scored and 29.4 allowed over 11 games. So the offense ranking around 20th by EPA flatters the November version. The run defense also looks better than it plays. It ranks 8th in rush EPA allowed and 3rd in missed-tackle rate, but opponents have run for 160 or more in several losses, mostly while milking leads built through the air. The real defensive identity is the pass defense, which ranks last in EPA allowed. It is 31st on short throws and 28th on deep ones, generates pressure at a bottom-eight rate, and has only 7 takeaways.

Where it goes from here depends on two things. One is whoever settles in at quarterback. The other is a soft run-in: Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Las Vegas all have losing records and bottom-half defenses. This team can steal one or two of those by controlling the clock. It ranks 4th in time of possession and 3rd in short-yardage conversion. But the ceiling is low until the secondary changes, and that is a roster question for the offseason, not December.

strengths.title: Clock control and short-yardage muscle
strengths.body: Arizona holds the ball as well as almost anyone. It ranks 4th in time of possession and converts short-yardage runs at the 3rd-best rate. That backs up an aggressive fourth-down approach that has gone for it when it can. This is the formula for keeping a bad pass defense off the field, and it holds up regardless of quarterback because it lives on the line and the backs.

strengths.title: Sure tackling, sound run fits
strengths.body: The defense ranks 3rd in missed-tackle rate and 8th in rush EPA allowed. On a per-play basis, the front does its job against the run. Some of that rank is game script: teams that are already ahead run to drain clock, and those carries grade out as low-value. Still, the tackling is a real trait, not an accident.

strengths.title: A true focal point in McBride
strengths.body: Trey McBride has drawn 113 targets, far more than anyone else on the roster. Whoever plays quarterback has an obvious first read. A backup can lean on that kind of volume, and it is the one piece of the passing game that has survived the quarterback changes.

concerns.title: The league's worst pass defense
concerns.body: Arizona ranks 32nd in pass EPA allowed, and it gets beaten in every way. It is 31st against short throws, 28th against deep ones, and 28th in explosive pass rate allowed. History says this is structural: the pass defense has ranked in the bottom quarter for most of the past four years. It will not be fixed in-season.

concerns.title: Offense collapsed after the QB change
concerns.body: Since Brissett stopped starting, the offense has scored 3, 6 and 7 points, and the Rams game produced -13.5 passing EPA. A line that ranks 27th in pressure rate allowed exposes backup quarterbacks quickly. Beck's back injury adds to the uncertainty. Until one passer settles in, scoring is the biggest single drag on the outlook.

concerns.title: No disruption, no stops in the red zone
concerns.body: The pass rush ranks 25th in pressure rate, and the defense has only 7 takeaways, 29th in the league. Offenses that reach the red zone score touchdowns 70% of the time. Without pressure or turnovers, a weak secondary has nothing to bail it out, so drives end in points rather than punts.

trend.note: Through eight weeks the results were uneven but competitive, including road wins at the Chargers, Rams and Cowboys. The last three games, all under backup quarterbacks, have been lopsided losses with single-digit scoring.

nextGame.headline: A 7.5-point home underdog needs McBride and the clock
nextGame.body:
Washington is a mediocre team that has lived on turnovers. It ranks 3rd in turnover differential per game and has 12 takeaways, with a middling offense around 20th in EPA. Its defense has a clear soft spot: it ranks dead last at containing opposing tight ends, and opponents throw against it more than almost anyone, with the 3rd-strongest pass funnel. It also does not finish drives well on defense, allowing red-zone touchdowns at a 29th-ranked rate. That sets up a path for an offense built around McBride and long possessions. The problem is the other side. Arizona's last-ranked pass defense meets a Washington passing game that has been efficient enough, and the Book's 7.5 points and 40.5 total suggest a grind that Washington controls.

Availability matters on both sides. Carson Beck is out with back spasms and guard Jon Gaines II is out with an ankle, which further thins a line that already struggles in protection. Jeremiyah Love is on IR, with his earliest return a week away. DT Zachary Carter remains on IR, and LB Cody Simon, a part-time player, is questionable with a calf. For Washington, Jayden Daniels has started every game but one. Starting corner Amik Robertson (98% of snaps) was inactive Monday with an ankle injury, and his status is worth checking. Tackle Laremy Tunsil is on IR and not expected back this regular season.

waysToWin.title: Feed McBride against a leaky TE defense
waysToWin.body: Washington ranks 32nd at holding top tight ends below their usual production. McBride is the offense's clear first read. Short, high-percentage throws to him spare a backup quarterback from reading coverage downfield and keep the chains moving.

waysToWin.title: Long drives that end in touchdowns
waysToWin.body: Arizona's possession game ranks 4th in time of possession, and Washington allows red-zone touchdowns at a 29th-ranked rate. If the Cardinals turn three or four long marches into sevens instead of field goals, they shorten the game and keep their secondary on the sideline.

waysToWin.title: Keep it close and let Washington blink
waysToWin.body: Washington has won only 30% of its one-score games. Its pass rush is also light on sacks, ranking 26th in sack rate, which gives a shaky quarterback and line a chance to survive. A low-scoring, fourth-quarter game is Arizona's best shot at an upset.

waysToLose.title: Daniels shreds the worst pass defense
waysToLose.body: Arizona ranks last in pass EPA allowed and 28th in explosive pass plays allowed. Washington's passing game is serviceable. A couple of chunk plays build a lead the Cardinals' offense has not been able to chase lately.

waysToLose.title: Backup QB gives away possessions
waysToLose.body: Washington's whole season leans on takeaways: 12 of them, with the 3rd-best turnover margin per game. A thin line facing a backup passer is exactly where those come from. Short fields would undo the clock-control plan.

waysToLose.title: Run game stalls, offense goes one-dimensional
waysToLose.body: Washington allows explosive runs at the 3rd-lowest rate. Without Love or Gaines, Arizona may not get the chunk runs that powered its Dallas win. Once the ground game stalls, the possession formula falls apart.

nextGame.watch: Who starts at quarterback, and whether McBride gets steady early targets against a defense that has been the league's worst against tight ends.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect more of the same at the extremes, with a little relief from the schedule. The pass defense is a multi-year problem and will keep allowing points in the high 20s to competent passing games. The offense's November collapse should ease somewhat once a quarterback settles in, but it will not return to the Brissett-era level without him. The clock-control and short-yardage traits are real and hold up week to week. They are the reason Arizona can be competitive against Philadelphia, the Jets, New Orleans and Las Vegas, all losing teams with bottom-half defenses.

There is no luck to regress in either direction. The record sits close to what the point differential implies, so wins will have to come from the matchups, not from bounces. A realistic finish is one to three more wins, most likely in the four home-heavy games against weak opponents before San Francisco closes the year.
swingFactors: Who wins the quarterback job, and Beck's back
Love's return from IR to restart the run game
Whether the pass rush can manufacture any takeaways

confidence.note: The profile is consistent with recent seasons, but the quarterback situation is unsettled and the efficiency rates appear to lag the latest games.
